title: Tom Garen's band: music as business, Ginny Simms and Tony Martin
summary: He left Milwaukee for Tom Garen's San Francisco band, which taught him music as a business and entertainment; Ginny Simms and Tony Martin were in it.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: And I joined another band and went to
Chicago, to join them, naturally. It was Tom Garen's band, a San Francisco band. And that was my first time in San Francisco.

Tom Garen was a very important influence on me, because I think he taught me a very great deal about music as a business. Tom was a businessman, and he was not in any sense of the word a musician you would look up to as an incentive to want to play better or something. But he did have a good sense of logic and he had a feeling for what the public would like. And the truth of the matter is that I would say that the majority of the bands during the late -- early '30s, actually, and even later, were really built on a pattern to find favor with an audience, and the quality of music really was secondary.

It was entirely up to the person's own judgment as to whether -- how important music was going to be in his particular band. And I learned a great deal from Tom, not because it was the best musical band I worked in, but because it was a great entertainment band. He had some very important people in the band, like Ginny Simms, a girl singer who later went to Kay Kyser's band. And we had another young man in the saxophone section, along with myself. His name was Tony Martin. It was then Al Morris, and later in the motion picture world he became known as Tony Martin.
And we all -- and there were two or three other

singers in the band who sang very well. And consequently, it was an entertaining unit, and that was the basis for the band, with some reasonably good music being played because we had a good arranger and a good musical director by the name of Gary Nottingham.
He wound up with the band here in San Francisco.
